blocks.text: **Multiplexing** combines multiple signals onto one shared medium to use capacity efficiently.

FDM splits by frequency (signals run simultaneously in different bands); TDM splits by time (signals take turns in slots). WDM is FDM applied to light in fibre. Statistical TDM allocates slots dynamically for bursty traffic — more efficient than fixed TDM.

mcqs.q: Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) shares a medium by:
options: Assigning each signal a time slot in turn
mcqs.explain: TDM interleaves signals in time, each getting slots; FDM uses separate frequency bands.

mcqs.q: WDM is essentially FDM applied to:
mcqs.explain: Wavelength Division Multiplexing sends multiple light 'colours' down one fibre — frequency division for light.

mcqs.q: Statistical TDM improves on fixed TDM by:
options: Allocating time slots on demand for bursty traffic
mcqs.explain: Dynamic slot allocation avoids wasting slots on idle channels, better for bursty data.

u:core-cn-9-nyquist-and-shannon-limits.title: Nyquist and Shannon limits
u:core-cn-9-nyquist-and-shannon-limits.summary: The formulas bounding data rate — noiseless (Nyquist) and noisy (Shannon) channels.

blocks.text: Two theorems bound the maximum data rate of a channel.

items: **Nyquist (noiseless channel)**: max rate = **2 × B × log2(L)** bits/sec, where B = bandwidth (Hz) and L = number of signal levels. More levels → more bits per symbol.
**Shannon (noisy channel)**: capacity = **B × log2(1 + S/N)** bits/sec, where S/N is the signal-to-noise ratio. This is the real-world ceiling regardless of levels.

blocks.text: Nyquist says you can gain rate by adding signal levels — but Shannon caps the true capacity based on noise. Beyond Shannon's limit, more levels just add errors, not throughput. The actual max rate is the lower of the two.
SNR is often given in decibels: SNR(dB) = 10·log10(S/N). Convert to the linear ratio before plugging into Shannon's formula.

mcqs.q: Shannon's channel capacity formula is:
mcqs.explain: Shannon's capacity for a noisy channel is B·log2(1 + S/N).

mcqs.q: In Nyquist's formula, increasing the number of signal levels L:
options: Increases the achievable data rate (more bits per symbol)
mcqs.explain: More levels encode more bits per symbol, raising the noiseless-channel rate — but Shannon still caps it.

mcqs.q: The true maximum data rate of a real channel is bounded by:
mcqs.explain: Noise limits real channels; beyond Shannon's capacity, adding levels just causes errors.

u:core-cn-10-framing.title: Framing
u:core-cn-10-framing.summary: The data link layer packages bits into frames with clear boundaries.

blocks.text: **Framing** is how the data link layer marks where each **frame** starts and ends in the raw bit stream, so the receiver can extract discrete units.

items: **Byte/character stuffing** — a special flag byte marks frame boundaries; if that byte appears in data, an escape byte is 'stuffed' before it.
**Bit stuffing** — a flag bit pattern (e.g. 01111110) marks boundaries; a 0 is inserted after five 1s in the data so the flag never appears accidentally.
Frames also carry addressing (MAC) and error-detection fields.

blocks.text: Framing solves 'where does one frame end and the next begin?'. Bit/byte stuffing prevents the frame-delimiter pattern from appearing inside the payload and being mistaken for a boundary.

mcqs.q: Bit stuffing prevents:
options: The frame delimiter (flag) pattern from appearing accidentally in the data
mcqs.explain: Inserting a 0 after five 1s ensures the flag pattern never occurs in the payload.

mcqs.q: Framing is a function of which layer?
mcqs.explain: The data link layer organises bits into frames with delimiters and addressing.

mcqs.q: Byte stuffing uses an escape byte to:
options: Distinguish a flag byte that appears within the data from a real frame boundary
mcqs.explain: When the flag byte occurs in data, an escape byte marks it as data, not a boundary.

u:core-cn-11-error-detection-parity-chec.title: Error detection: parity, checksum, CRC
u:core-cn-11-error-detection-parity-chec.summary: Redundant bits that let the receiver detect corruption — from weak parity to strong CRC.

blocks.text: **Error detection** adds redundant bits so the receiver can tell if data was corrupted in transit.

rows: One bit making the count of 1s even/odd
Weak — misses even numbers of bit errors
Sum of data words, sent along; re-summed at receiver
Strong — catches burst errors; used in Ethernet

blocks.text: Strength ordering: parity (weakest, misses even-count errors) < checksum < CRC (strongest, great at burst errors). Ethernet uses CRC (FCS field). These detect errors; they don't correct them (except Hamming/FEC).

mcqs.q: A single parity bit fails to detect:
options: An even number of bit errors
mcqs.explain: Parity flips only on an odd number of errors, so even-count errors go undetected.

mcqs.q: Which error-detection method is strongest and used in Ethernet?
mcqs.explain: CRC via polynomial division is robust against burst errors and used as Ethernet's frame check sequence.

mcqs.q: Error-detection codes like CRC allow the receiver to:
options: Detect that corruption occurred (then request retransmission)
mcqs.explain: Detection codes flag corruption; correction (e.g. via ARQ retransmission or FEC) is a separate step.

u:core-cn-12-error-correction-hamming-co.title: Error correction: Hamming code
u:core-cn-12-error-correction-hamming-co.summary: Add parity bits at power-of-two positions to locate and fix a single-bit error.

blocks.text: **Forward error correction** lets the receiver **fix** errors without retransmission. The **Hamming code** can **correct a single-bit error** by adding parity bits at positions that are powers of two (1, 2, 4, 8…).

items: Each parity bit covers a specific set of positions; together their results form a binary number pointing at the erroneous bit.
For k parity bits and m data bits, they must satisfy **2^k >= m + k + 1**.
Basic Hamming corrects 1-bit errors and detects 2-bit errors (with an extra overall parity, SECDED).

blocks.text: The clever part: the parity bits, read together, give the binary position of the flipped bit — so the receiver knows exactly which bit to invert. This is worthwhile where retransmission is costly (deep space, storage).

mcqs.q: A basic Hamming code can:
mcqs.explain: Hamming(7,4)-style codes locate and correct one bit error (and detect two with SECDED).

mcqs.q: In a Hamming code, parity bits are placed at positions that are:
mcqs.explain: Power-of-two positions let the parity checks combine to indicate the error's binary position.

mcqs.q: The relation between k parity bits and m data bits is:
mcqs.explain: The parity bits must be enough to identify every bit position plus the no-error case.

u:core-cn-13-stop-and-wait-arq.title: Stop-and-wait ARQ
u:core-cn-13-stop-and-wait-arq.summary: Send one frame, wait for its ACK, then send the next — simple but inefficient.

blocks.text: **ARQ (Automatic Repeat reQuest)** uses acknowledgements and timeouts for reliable delivery. **Stop-and-wait** is the simplest: the sender transmits one frame, then **waits for an ACK** before sending the next; on timeout it retransmits.

items: Uses a 1-bit sequence number to detect duplicate frames (from a lost ACK).
**Inefficient** on high-bandwidth or long-delay links: the sender sits idle during the round trip.
Efficiency = 1 / (1 + 2a), where a = propagation time / transmission time.

blocks.text: Stop-and-wait is correct but wastes the link: only one frame is in flight, so on a 'long fat' pipe (high bandwidth × delay) the sender is idle most of the time. Sliding-window protocols fix this by allowing multiple in-flight frames.

mcqs.q: In stop-and-wait ARQ, the sender transmits the next frame:
options: Only after receiving the ACK for the previous frame (or a timeout)
mcqs.explain: Only one frame is outstanding; the sender waits for its ACK before sending the next.

mcqs.q: Stop-and-wait is inefficient mainly on:
options: Long-delay / high-bandwidth links where the sender idles during the round trip
mcqs.explain: With a large bandwidth-delay product, one-frame-at-a-time leaves the link mostly idle.

mcqs.q: The sequence number in stop-and-wait needs how many bits?
mcqs.explain: A single bit (alternating 0/1) suffices to distinguish a frame from its retransmission/duplicate.

u:core-cn-14-go-back-n.title: Go-Back-N
u:core-cn-14-go-back-n.summary: A sliding-window protocol that retransmits everything from a lost frame onward.

blocks.text: **Go-Back-N (GBN)** is a sliding-window ARQ: the sender can have up to **N** unacknowledged frames in flight. The receiver accepts frames **only in order** and discards anything out of order.

items: Uses **cumulative ACKs** (ACK n means all frames up to n received).
On a lost/errored frame, the sender must **go back and retransmit that frame and all subsequent ones** — even correctly-received ones are discarded by the receiver.
Receiver window size = 1 (in-order only). Sender window <= 2^k − 1 for a k-bit sequence number.

blocks.text: GBN keeps the receiver simple (in-order, no buffering) at the cost of bandwidth: one loss forces retransmission of a whole window. Efficient on low-error links, wasteful when errors are frequent.

mcqs.q: In Go-Back-N, when a frame is lost, the sender retransmits:
options: That frame and all frames sent after it
mcqs.explain: The receiver discards out-of-order frames, so the sender resends from the lost frame onward.

mcqs.q: The Go-Back-N receiver window size is:
mcqs.explain: GBN receivers accept frames strictly in order, so the receive window is 1.

mcqs.q: Go-Back-N uses which kind of acknowledgements?
mcqs.explain: A cumulative ACK n confirms all frames through n have been received in order.

u:core-cn-15-selective-repeat.title: Selective Repeat
u:core-cn-15-selective-repeat.summary: Retransmit only the lost frames; the receiver buffers out-of-order ones.

blocks.text: **Selective Repeat (SR)** improves on Go-Back-N by retransmitting **only the specific frames that were lost/errored**. The receiver **buffers out-of-order** frames and individually ACKs each correct one.

items: Both sender and receiver have windows of size N; the receiver buffers and reorders.
More efficient than GBN on error-prone links (no needless retransmission).
More complex (receiver buffering, per-frame ACKs). Requires **window size <= 2^(k-1)** for a k-bit sequence number to avoid ambiguity.

blocks.text: SR vs GBN: SR resends only what's lost (bandwidth-efficient) but needs a buffering receiver and per-frame ACKs (complex). The window constraint (<= half the sequence space) prevents old and new frames being confused.

mcqs.q: In Selective Repeat, on a single lost frame the sender retransmits:
mcqs.explain: SR resends just the missing frame; the receiver has buffered the others.

mcqs.q: Compared to Go-Back-N, Selective Repeat requires the receiver to:
options: Buffer out-of-order frames and reorder them
mcqs.explain: SR receivers buffer out-of-order frames, which is more complex but avoids retransmitting good frames.

mcqs.q: For a k-bit sequence number, the Selective Repeat window size must be at most:
mcqs.explain: SR needs window <= half the sequence-number space to avoid confusing new frames with retransmissions.

u:core-cn-16-sliding-window-and-efficien.title: Sliding window and efficiency
u:core-cn-16-sliding-window-and-efficien.summary: Keep multiple frames in flight to fill the pipe — efficiency depends on window vs bandwidth-delay.

blocks.text: The **sliding window** protocol lets the sender transmit up to **W** frames before needing an ACK, keeping the link busy. As ACKs arrive, the window 'slides' forward.
Efficiency

items: Let **a = propagation time / transmission time**. Stop-and-wait efficiency = 1/(1+2a).
Sliding-window efficiency = **W/(1+2a)** (capped at 1 when W >= 1+2a).
To fully use the link, the window must cover the **bandwidth-delay product** — enough frames to keep sending until the first ACK returns.

blocks.text: The goal: size the window so W >= 1 + 2a, i.e. enough in-flight data to cover a full round trip (the bandwidth-delay product). Then the sender never idles waiting for ACKs and reaches ~100% link utilisation.
Bandwidth-delay product = bandwidth × round-trip time = the amount of data 'in the pipe'. TCP's window must match it to fill a high-speed, high-latency link.

mcqs.q: To keep a link fully utilised, the sliding window size should cover:
options: The bandwidth-delay product (data in flight over a round trip)
mcqs.explain: A window matching the bandwidth-delay product keeps the sender transmitting until the first ACK returns.

mcqs.q: Sliding-window efficiency with window W and a = Tp/Tt is:
mcqs.explain: Multiple in-flight frames multiply stop-and-wait efficiency by W, up to full utilisation.

mcqs.q: The bandwidth-delay product represents:
options: The amount of data that can be 'in the pipe' at once
mcqs.explain: It's bandwidth × RTT — how much data is in transit, which the window must cover for full use.
